Stage 3 · Reading

What you will have done with the time

Most people plan their money forty years ahead and their free time about forty minutes ahead.

⏳💰
1 · Before you read. Imagine you were given six free hours every day, for the rest of your life. How would that feel after a month?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

What you will have done with the time

Written for this course, from Sharif, Mogilner & Hershfield, ‘Having too little or too much time is linked to lower subjective well-being’, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 121(4), 2021, and the American Time Use Survey.

1Ask somebody where their money will be in thirty years and they will usually have an answer. There will be a pension, possibly an inheritance, some vague expectation about healthcare costs, and a figure they have looked up more than once. Ask the same person how they will be spending their Tuesday evenings in 2055 and the question sounds absurd. We think ahead about money as a matter of course. We take time for granted, and by the time we notice, we will already have spent most of it.

2The arithmetic is not complicated. If you are thirty now, you will have lived roughly eleven thousand days and, on current life expectancy in most of Europe, you will live perhaps another nineteen thousand. Subtract sleep and work and the commute, and the discretionary hours — the ones nobody else has a claim on — come to something in the region of four a day. By the time you are seventy you will have accumulated more than fifty thousand of them. That is a larger fund than most people’s savings, and almost nobody manages it.

3The obvious conclusion is that more free time must be better, and the research says otherwise. In 2021 three researchers at Wharton and UCLA examined responses from more than 35,000 Americans, most of them drawn from the American Time Use Survey, and ran two experiments of their own. Well-being rose as daily discretionary time increased, levelled off after about two hours, and then began to fall again beyond roughly five. Too little time produces stress. Too much, the authors argue, produces something else: a lacking sense of productivity and purpose.

4That finding has an obvious application, and almost everyone will have met it by the time they stop working. Anyone who retires at sixty-five will be handling eight or nine unstructured hours a day, every day, for perhaps twenty years. By the end of the first decade they will have spent more waking hours in retirement than in the whole of secondary school and university combined. The people who cope best with that, according to the same research, are not the ones with the most flexibility but the ones whose extra hours go into something they consider worthwhile — and time spent with other people counts.

5The practical advice that follows is duller than it sounds. Do not while away the hours waiting for a better use of them to appear; it will not. Do not kill time and call it resting, because the two feel quite different afterwards. Take your time over things that repay it, and put a limit on the things that do not. Above all, stay in contact: the friendships people lose are almost never ended deliberately, and once you have lost touch with somebody for five years, you will usually have lost them for good. In ten years you will still be meaning to call them.

6None of this is an argument for treating leisure as another job. People who throw their money around are considered foolish; people who throw their hours around are considered normal, and the only real difference is that nobody sends you a statement. Next Sunday will be disappearing in exactly the same way, and by Monday you will have forgotten what happened to it. In twenty years’ time you will not be remembering the evenings you filled efficiently. You will be remembering whether you made the most of the ones that mattered.

Text A · The fund nobody manages

Written for this course, using life-expectancy and time-use arithmetic from the American Time Use Survey.

Ask somebody where their money will be in thirty years and they will usually have an answer. There will be a pension, possibly an inheritance, some vague expectation about healthcare costs, and a figure they have looked up more than once. Ask the same person how they will be spending their Tuesday evenings in 2055 and the question sounds absurd. We think ahead about money as a matter of course. We take time for granted, and by the time we notice, we will already have spent most of it.

The arithmetic is not complicated. If you are thirty now, you will have lived roughly eleven thousand days and, on current life expectancy in most of Europe, you will live perhaps another nineteen thousand. Subtract sleep and work and the commute, and the discretionary hours — the ones nobody else has a claim on — come to something in the region of four a day. By the time you are seventy you will have accumulated more than fifty thousand of them. By then you will also have been working for something like forty-five years, and you will still not have decided what the evenings are for. That is a larger fund than most people’s savings, and almost nobody manages it.

People who throw their money around are considered foolish; people who throw their hours around are considered normal, and the only real difference is that nobody sends you a statement. A bank will tell you what you spent last month and what it left you with. Nothing performs that service for a Sunday afternoon. Next Sunday will be disappearing in exactly the same way, and by Monday you will have forgotten what happened to it. This is why the hours disappear without an argument: not because anyone decides to waste them, but because nothing in the system makes the loss visible while there is still time to do something about it.

Text B · The two-to-five-hour finding

Written for this course, from Sharif, Mogilner & Hershfield, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 121(4), 2021.

The obvious conclusion is that more free time must be better, and the research says otherwise. In 2021 three researchers at Wharton and UCLA examined responses from more than 35,000 Americans, most drawn from the American Time Use Survey, plus two experiments of their own. Well-being rose as daily discretionary time increased, levelled off after about two hours, and then began to fall again beyond roughly five. Too little time produces stress. Too much, the authors argue, produces something else: a lacking sense of productivity and purpose. Most readers will be living somewhere inside that curve.

Almost everyone will have met that finding by the time they stop working. Anyone who retires at sixty-five will be handling eight or nine unstructured hours a day, every day, for perhaps twenty years. By the end of the first decade they will have spent more waking hours in retirement than in the whole of secondary school and university combined. The people who cope best, according to the same research, are not those with the most flexibility but those whose extra hours go into something worthwhile — and time with others counts. By seventy-five they will have made that decision some three thousand times.

The practical advice that follows is duller than it sounds. Do not while away the hours waiting for a better use to appear; it will not. Do not kill time and call it resting, because the two feel quite different afterwards. Take your time over things that repay it, and put a limit on the things that do not. Above all, stay in contact: the friendships people lose are almost never ended deliberately, and once you have lost touch with somebody for five years you will usually have lost them for good, while still meaning to call. In twenty years you will not be remembering the evenings you filled efficiently, but whether you made the most of the ones that mattered.

4 · One evening, four ways of describing it.
At eight I will cook dinner.  →  the cooking starts at eight.

1 · Read the explanation.
Name the future point first

Both forms in this lesson need a point in the future to work from — this time next week, by June, when you arrive. Once that point is fixed, you have a choice: say what will be going on at it, or say what will already be over before it.

The future continuous (will be + -ing) puts the listener inside the action at that moment. At eight I will be cooking means that if you came round at eight you would find me in the kitchen. It has two further jobs. It describes things expected to happen anyway, in the normal course of events — I will be seeing her on Thursday, so I can ask then — and it asks about plans without pressing for a decision: Will you be using the car tonight? is a question; Will you use the car tonight? sounds like a request.

The future perfect (will have + past participle) stands at the future point and looks back at something finished before it. By June we will have finished the course. The word that most often introduces it is by: by then, by March, by the time you arrive. Note the difference between by and in: in June dates the event, by June only sets the limit it has to fall inside.

The future perfect continuous (will have been + -ing) answers how long at that future point: In September she will have been working here for ten years. Use it with for and a length of time, not with a number of completed things.

The two questions to ask
  • At that moment, or before it? at six → will be doing  ·  by six → will have done
  • Finished, or measured in hours? will have written three reports  ·  will have been writing for six hours
  • State verbs stay simple: will have known, will have been — not will have been knowing.
  • After by the time, when, before, as soon as, the verb is present: by the time you arrive.

Two things to watch

1 — No will inside the time clause. The clause that names the future point uses a present form: By the time you arrive, the talk will have started — never by the time you will arrive. Exactly the same rule you met with when and as soon as in the last lesson.

2 — Will have been is not a past passive. She will have finished the report is what she does; the report will have been finished is the passive of it. She will have been finished is a common slip and means nothing. Keep will have been + -ing for duration only.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
Standing in the future and looking around

Both forms start by naming a point in the future and then describe it from the inside. will be + -ing shows an action in progress at that point: This time next week I will be sitting on a train to Almaty. will have + past participle shows an action finished before it: By June we will have finished the whole course. The point itself is usually given by this time next week, by June, by the time you arrive, by then.

The future continuous does a second job that has nothing to do with progress: it presents something as part of the normal run of things, with no intention behind it. I will be seeing her on Thursday, so I can ask then means you were going to see her anyway. That is why it makes such a neutral question: Will you be using the car this evening? asks without asking for anything, where Are you going to use the car? sounds like the beginning of a request.

Finished by then, and how long by then

The future perfect needs a point to be measured against, and that point is what by supplies: By the end of the month, By the time you arrive, By then. Without one the form floats: I will have finished on its own says almost nothing. Note the time clause again: By the time you arrive, the talk will have started — present, not future, after by the time.

will have been + -ing gives the length of something at that future point: In June she will have been working here for ten years. Compare it with the plain future perfect: she will have trained two people counts results; she will have been training people for a decade measures duration.

Errors to watch: By the time you will arrive → By the time you arrive · I will have finished by tomorrow the report → word order: I will have finished the report by tomorrow · This time next week I will sit on a train → will be sitting · In June she will work here for ten years → will have been working.

Stage 5 · Speaking & WritingWriting

The next two hundred hours

Two free hours a week for two years comes to about two hundred hours. This is a plan for them, and a defence of it.

The brief

You have roughly two hundred free hours over the next two years, on top of everything you already do. Decide what will have happened to them by the end, and be ready to say what you will be doing with them in the meantime. The plan has to survive one bad month, one expensive month, and one month when somebody else needs your evenings.

1 · Read the model.
Model · a plan for two hundred hours

By this time in two years I will have spent about two hundred free hours on one thing, and I would rather choose it now than find out afterwards what it was. The thing is technical drawing. By the end of next year I will have finished the two online modules, and by the following summer I will have been drawing regularly for two years, which is roughly the point at which people stop being embarrassed to show anybody.

An ordinary week will not look dramatic. On Tuesday evenings I will be working through a module, and one Sunday a month I will be sitting in a room with three other people doing the same thing. That Sunday is the part I would defend first, because it is also the reason I will not have lost touch with two of them by then.

The flexibility is deliberate: two evenings a week and no more, so that a bad month at work costs me the month and not the plan. I will not have spent much money either. I refuse to throw money around on equipment for something I might have abandoned by March, so the good paper waits until the second year. By the time the second year starts, I will already know whether I am still interested. If I am not, that is the answer, and I will stop.
